### First rows of a random Young diagram under the $q$-Plancherel measure

Let us suppose $q<1$. In this paper, we prove a law of large numbers and a central limit theorem for the vector containing the lengths of the first $k$ rows of a random diagram under the $q$-Plancherel measure $M_{n,q}$. Note that Theorem [\[th:first_order_as_rows\]](#th:first_order_as_rows){reference-type="ref" reference="th:first_order_as_rows"} implies that the first $k$ rows contain asymptotically $(1-q^k) \times n$ boxes, therefore describing the length of theses rows gives a good description of the diagram. As $M_{n,q^{-1}}(\lambda')=M_{n,q}(\lambda)$ (this follows from Definition [\[def_measure\]](#def_measure){reference-type="ref" reference="def_measure"}), in the case $q>1$, our result gives the asymptotic behavior of the columns, which are, in this case, the relevant quantities.

::: theorem
[]{#th:first_order_as_rows label="th:first_order_as_rows"} Suppose $q<1$. If $\lambda=(\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \cdots)$ denotes a Young diagram of size $n$ under the $q$-Plancherel measure (*cf.* figure [1](#fig:ex_diag_qplanch){reference-type="ref" reference="fig:ex_diag_qplanch"}), then $$\begin{aligned}
\forall i \geq 1,\,\,\,\frac{\lambda_i}{n} & \longrightarrow_{M_{n,q}} (1-q)\,q^{i-1};
\end{aligned}$$ where the arrow $\to_{M_{n,q}}$ means convergence in probability.
:::

::: theorem
[]{#th:second_order_as_rows label="th:second_order_as_rows"} Under the same hypothesis, if $Y_{n,q,i}$ is the rescaled deviation $$\sqrt{n}\,\left(\frac{\lambda_i}{n} - (1-q)\,q^{i-1}\right),$$ then we have convergence of the finite-dimensional laws of the random process $(Y_{n,q,i})_{i \geq 1}$ towards those of a gaussian process $(Y_{q,i})_{i \geq 1}$ with: $$\mathbb{E}[Y_{q,i}]=0 \quad ;\quad \mathbb{E}[Y_{q,i}^2]=(1-q)\,q^{i-1}-(1-q)^2\,q^{2(i-1)}\quad ;\quad 
\mathrm{cov}(Y_{q,i},Y_{q,j})=-(1-q)^2\,q^{i+j-2}.$$
:::

In particular, two different coordinates $Y_{q,i}$ and $Y_{q,j}$ are negatively correlated. For the readers not accustomed to the topology of convergence in law, let us give a more concrete version of Theorem [\[th:second_order_as_rows\]](#th:second_order_as_rows){reference-type="ref" reference="th:second_order_as_rows"}. Given $\varepsilon>0$ and for any positive real numbers $x_1,\ldots,x_r$, Theorem [\[th:second_order_as_rows\]](#th:second_order_as_rows){reference-type="ref" reference="th:second_order_as_rows"} ensures that, for $n$ big enough: $$\left|\mathbb{P}\left[ \forall i \in \left[\!\left[1,r \right]\!\right],\,\, |\lambda_i- (1-q)\,q^{i-1}\,n|\leq x_i\,\sqrt{n} \right]-\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^r\,\det Q}}\,\int_{-x_{1}}^{x_1}\cdots\int_{-x_{r}}^{x_r}\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{{}^tXQ^{-1}X}{2}}\,dX\right| \leq \varepsilon,$$ where $Q$ is the symmetric matrix with coefficients $Q_{ij}=\delta_{ij}\,(1-q)\,q^{i-1}-(1-q)^2\,q^{i+j-2}$. This matrix is positive definite because of the Hadamard rule (in each column, the diagonal coefficient is positive and strictly bigger than the sum of the absolute values of the other coordinates).

### Other measures

As mentioned in paragraph [\[subsect:background\]](#subsect:background){reference-type="ref" reference="subsect:background"}, our method is quite general. We can establish limit shape theorems with different rescalings. As an example, in paragraph [\[sect:schur-weyl\]](#sect:schur-weyl){reference-type="ref" reference="sect:schur-weyl"}, we introduce some natural probability measures on Young diagrams. We obtain the following result:

::: theorem
[]{#prop:SW_asymptotic_shape label="prop:SW_asymptotic_shape"} Let $(\lambda_n)_{n}$ be the sequence of random Young diagrams described in paragraph [\[subsect:def_SW\]](#subsect:def_SW){reference-type="ref" reference="subsect:def_SW"}. We assume $N \sim c\cdot n^\alpha$ with $\alpha <1/2$.

Then, for each $\varepsilon, \eta > 0$, there exists an integer $n_0$ such that, for each $n \geq n_0$, the border of the diagram $\lambda_n$ is, after rescaling and with probability greater than $1 - \varepsilon$, contained in the hatched area:

<figure id="fig:rectangle">
<div class="center">
<p><span><span>(-2,-2)(100,45) (0,25)(0,22)(58,22)(58,0)(90,0)(90,3)(62,3)(62,25) (90,0)(90,3) (-2,0)(95,0) (0,-2)(0,40) (105,0)<span><span class="math inline"> × <em>n</em><sup>1 − <em>α</em></sup></span></span> (0,45)<span><span class="math inline"> × <em>n</em><sup><em>α</em></sup></span></span> (60,-3)<span><span class="math inline"><em>c</em></span></span> (-4,25)<span><span class="math inline"><em>c</em><sup>−1</sup></span></span> (30,25)(30,22) (30,28)<span><span class="math inline"><em>c</em><sup>−1</sup><em>η</em></span></span> (58,13)(62,13) (66,13)<span><span class="math inline"><em>c</em><em>η</em></span></span> (-1,25)(0,25) (60,-1)(60,1) </span></span></p>
</div>
<figcaption>Limit shape of a rescaled random diagram under the Schur-Weyl measure of parameters <span class="math inline"><em>c</em> &gt; 0</span> and <span class="math inline"><em>α</em> &lt; 1/2</span>.<span id="fig:rectangle" label="fig:rectangle"></span></figcaption>
</figure>
:::

Unfortunately, one can not use this to give the precise behavior of the first row of the diagram. The only result we have is the following (which is a consequence of Proposition [\[prop:cv_powersums_encore\]](#prop:cv_powersums_encore){reference-type="ref" reference="prop:cv_powersums_encore"}):

::: proposition
[]{#prop:SW_first_row label="prop:SW_first_row"} Let $\lambda_n$ be the sequence of random diagrams described in paragraph [\[subsect:def_SW\]](#subsect:def_SW){reference-type="ref" reference="subsect:def_SW"}. Let us assume that $N \sim c \, n^\alpha$ with $\alpha <1/2$. For any $\varepsilon > 0$, one has $\lambda_1=o(n^{1-\alpha+\varepsilon})$ in probability.
:::

### Longest increasing subsequence {#subsect:ss_suite_croissante}

It is well-known that the length of the first row of a Young diagram of size $n$ under Plancherel measure has the same distribution as the length of the longest increasing subsequence of a random permutation of size $n$ (under the uniform distribution). Indeed, the shape of the tableaux obtained by the Robinson-Schensted bijection defines a map $$\mathfrak{S}_n \longrightarrow \{\lambda \vdash n\},$$ which sends the length of the longest increasing subsequence on the length of the first row of $\lambda$. The image of the uniform distribution on $\mathfrak{S}_n$ is the Plancherel measure on Young diagrams of size $n$, and this explains the aforementioned result.

Our results on the $q$-Plancherel measure can also be interpreted in the context of longest increasing subsequences. Indeed, E. Strahov [@Stra08] has noticed that the $q$-Plancherel measure is the image by the map above of the probability measure defined by $$\forall \ \sigma,\ \mathbb{P}[\sigma ] = Z \cdot q^{\mathop{\mathrm{imaj}}(\sigma)},$$ where $\mathop{\mathrm{imaj}}(\sigma)$, called major index, is the sum of the integers $i$ between $1$ and $n-1$ such that $\sigma(i)>\sigma(i+1)$ and $Z=1/\{n!\}_q$ is the normalization constant such that the probabilities sum to $1$. So Theorems [\[th:first_order_as_rows\]](#th:first_order_as_rows){reference-type="ref" reference="th:first_order_as_rows"} and [\[th:second_order_as_rows\]](#th:second_order_as_rows){reference-type="ref" reference="th:second_order_as_rows"} imply the following:

::: theorem
Let $q$ be a real in $]0,1[$ and $n$ an integer. Consider the distribution on permutations such that the probability of picking a permutation $\sigma$ is proportional to $q^{\mathop{\mathrm{imaj}}(\sigma)}$. The length $\ell(\sigma)$ of the longest increasing subsequence of a permutation under this distribution is equivalent in probability to $n(1-q)$. Moreover, the rescaled deviation $(\ell(\sigma) - n(1-q))/\sqrt{n}$ converges in law towards a centered normal law of variance $q(1-q)$.
:::

As mentioned in subsection [\[subsect:def_SW\]](#subsect:def_SW){reference-type="ref" reference="subsect:def_SW"}, the measure considered in section [\[sect:schur-weyl\]](#sect:schur-weyl){reference-type="ref" reference="sect:schur-weyl"} is the image by the RSK algorithm of the uniform distribution on words of length $n$ with letters from $1$ to $N$. So, Proposition [\[prop:SW_first_row\]](#prop:SW_first_row){reference-type="ref" reference="prop:SW_first_row"} implies:

::: corollary
[]{#th:SW_lis_upbound label="th:SW_lis_upbound"} Fix $c>0$ and $0<\alpha <1/2$. Let $\ell$ be the length of the longest non-decreasing subsequence of a random word with $n$ letters between $1$ and $c \cdot \lfloor n^\alpha \rfloor$. When $n$ tends to infinity, one has in probability: $\ell = o(n^{1-\alpha+\varepsilon})$.
:::
